source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
description: Queen of the night is a tropical, epiphytic or lithophytic, spineless cactus grown for its large, fragrant flowers. It is native to Central America and thrives in wet tropical and subtropical climates rather than in dry, arid areas. In its native habitat, it is found growing on other plants or trees as well as rocks and may grow up to 10 feet tall. This member of the cactus family (Cactaceae) is the most frequently cultivated species in the genus. The species epithet is compounded from the Greek words oxy -, meaning "sour," and -petalum , meaning "petal." It presumably accurately describes their taste, although this plant is not known to have edible flowers. This plant requires bright, indirect light and protection from the harsh afternoon sun. Give this plant a well-drained average succulent or cactus potting mix with added sand or perlite. Soak the soil completely when watering, and water regularly during the spring and summer. Allow the top of the soil to dry out between watering. Reduce the water schedule during the fall and winter when growth is slowed. It is not frost-tolerant and prefers temperatures between 50 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit. It thrives in high humidity, but can tolerate dry air. Repotting may be required every 2 or 3 years. The queen of the night can be easily propagated by stem cuttings. The plant is an erect, sprawling, and spineless cactus. It has long, flat, green segmented stems or leaf-like branches (called phylloclades) that may have wavy or lobed edges and measure up to 16 inches long. The flowers are white, fragrant, waterlily-like like and measure 12 inches long and 8 inches wide. They are night-blooming and wither by the next morning. They typically bloom in the late spring to early summer; however, houseplants tend to bloom sporadically. In the wild, the flowers are pollinated by bats and moths. After flowering, purplish-red fruits are produced that are edible. The queen of the night has slightly different growing needs than other cacti or succulents. If you are up for the challenge, you will be rewarded with a beautiful and unique houseplant. Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems: Common insects include mealybugs, spider mites, and scale. The plant is susceptible to root rot in the presence of overwatering or poorly drained soil. Powdery mildew can occur if the air circulation is poor. Exposure to direct sunlight can cause sunburn. Uses (Ethnobotany): Used in herbal medicine esp. in Asia and India
Distribution: Native: Belize, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, and Nicaragua. Distribution: Brazil, China, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Leeward Islands, Marquesas, Marshall Islands, Puerto Rico, Society Islands, Tuamotu, Tubuai Island, Venezuelan Antilles, Vietnam, and Windward Islands.
Wildlife Value: In their native habitat, flowers are pollinated by bats and moths.
Light: Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)
Fruit Description: A bright purplish-red fruit similar to pitaya or dragon fruit. The inner flesh is white and contains small black seeds. It is oblong and angled, up to 6 inches long and 3 inches wide. Fruits are rarely produced.
Flower Description: Huge, showy, white flowers with fragrant blooms with 25 to 30 petals. The sepals may be yellowish or pinkish. They grow on long floral tubes that emerge from the cladode margins. They bloom at night annually, each flower lasting a few hours.
Leaf Description: No true leaves but flattened, leaf-like stems (phylloclades) with crenate and wavy margins. See stem information.
Stem Description: What appear to be leaves are phylloclades, i.e., long, flattened stems with more than one node. The phylloclades function like a leaf. They are elliptic with undulate or crenate margins. The stems can reach lengths of up to 20 feet. The flowers grow from the nodes on the margins of these stems.
